item.title: Why Overthinking Keeps You Stuck
item.description:
Unconscious

Why Overthinking Keeps You Stuck

The most articulate and logical people are often the most immobilized.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Some problems yield to thinking, but existential situations do not.
  • Being logically right and being stuck are compatible.
  • Notice what opens or closes in you through your felt sense.

Identifying details have been changed to protect client confidentiality.

He could explain it in under five minutes. Several years in a serious professional role, the high salary, the first home he was saving toward, the market being what it is, and the reasonable thing being what the reasonable thing so obviously was. He had told this story to his partner, family, friends, and to himself in the middle of the night. Every listener agreed with him, because they were also being reasonable.

Source: Timothy Barlin / Unsplash

He told it to me the same way each week, in the manner of a man laying out evidence. Then, later, he would often come apart in session. He could not get himself out of bed on work mornings, or his body would lock before the drive to the office, engine running, hands on the wheel, going nowhere. A heaviness would come over him on ordinary Tuesdays and relentlessly consume him.

The ego is not the only voice

Depth psychology begins with a claim that makes most people raised in modern times uncomfortable: The part of us doing the talking is not the whole of us.

The ego is our maker of coherence; it takes the raw weather of a life and shapes it into something a person can live inside, and coherence is how the unbearable becomes survivable. But psyche is older and wider than the story, and it is under no obligation to agree with your rational mind.

Psyche means soul. Psychotherapy, read plainly, is a tending of the soul, named long before we reduced it to the management of symptoms. Soul here belongs to no church and requires no dogma. It is the name for the depth in a person, which has its own weather and its own view of the life you have arranged.

Jung's essential contribution was that the unconscious is not a cellar where discarded things are kept.1 The depths within us are alive and autonomous; they hold their own position, and they will state it in whatever language remains open. A dream, an image or fantasy that will not leave, the feeling world, or a body that will not get out of the car.

So, a person can be entirely logical and entirely stuck at the same time. The stuckness is not a failure of thinking; it is dissent, arriving from a part of him that was never authentically consulted, in a language he was never taught to hear.

What thinking cannot metabolize

There are problems, and there are situations, and the difference matters. A problem yields to good thinking: a scheduling conflict, mortgage, or maybe a difficult hire at work. An existential situation does not. A terminal diagnosis, the marriage that has quietly emptied out, a crisis of faith, estrangement from a sibling, or the death of a child: these are what some existential philosophers have called choiceless situations, and what the rest of us simply call life.2 No further explanation resolves them, because insufficient explanation was never the cause of the anguish.

When we keep bringing thought to what thought cannot carry, the reasoning mind, meant to be one voice among several, begins to behave as though it were the whole choir. A man can then tell the story again, exactly as well as the first time, and nothing moves.

Living in one's head is usually an intelligent adaptation, made early, in a household where feeling was unsafe or unwelcome, but adaptations outlive their usefulness. As the Jungian analyst James Hollis puts it, our adaptive loyalty to what we received from our childhood environment can become an unconscious subversion of the soul's integrity.3

If you can't feel it, you can't heal it

Feelings are, in Hollis's phrasing, autonomous responses of the organism to how things are going from its own perspective.3 We can ignore them, project them onto other people, or bury them under productivity, but we never choose the initial feeling. Something in us goes on speaking whether or not we are willing to hear it, and trust me when I say it does not tire. This is why depth-oriented, holistic, and other embodied psychotherapies place the felt sense at the centre of the work: There is no other way to carry what a life gives you.

Consulting the rest of yourself

None of this asks you to abandon reason or critical thinking; you will need a clear mind to receive whatever the depths send up. It asks only that you widen the circle of what gets consulted: felt sense, emotion, intuition, sensation, imagination, dream, fantasy, vision, etc. Most of us were taught to hear all of it as random static, when it is often the only thing in us sensitive enough to catch the questions that matter.

Here is a rough test, simpler than it sounds. When you consider a possible next step, slow down and notice what happens in your body. Not what you conclude about it—what happens in you. Does something open, or does something close? Is there a small quickening, a sense of aliveness, even where the step frightens you? Or a subtle deadening, a heaviness, a going-grey, even where the step is entirely defensible on paper?

If it enlivens, take it seriously; if it deadens, get curious about it, however neatly it fits the story you have been telling. This is no shortcut to a good outcome, but it is a way of staying in relationship with yourself while you make an intentional choice. It is harder than it sounds, because the soul speaks quietly while the world is very loud.

A slow burn

He stayed with the work for more than a year, on a question he had arrived certain he could settle in a few days.

What changed first was not the job. He stopped treating the frozen mornings as malfunction and began treating them as something to listen to. He started journalling his feelings and tracking bodily sensations, awkwardly at first. Then his feeling world broke open, overwhelming him, and he took several weeks away from work. Yet, in that rest, he went further inward, and the depression that had been consuming him began to lift as he reconnected wholeheartedly with his own psyche and body.

He is no longer the same man sitting in a running car with his hands on the wheel. When he speaks about the future, there is something in the room that was not there before, and he has access to a new realm of creative possibilities. He recently liberated himself externally from his toxic corporate job.

Going inward is not a retreat from the world; it is what makes meeting the world possible.
